faqs.q: Do alligators live in Wilmington's lakes and ponds?
faqs.a: Yes. Greenfield Lake, the Cape Fear River, and retention ponds across the city are alligator habitat, and animals bask and move through the system especially in spring and early summer. Never feed one — it is unlawful in North Carolina — keep pets away from pond edges, and keep your distance. Only an Alligator Control Agent under a per-animal permit from the NC Wildlife Resources Commission can handle one; report concerns to the Wildlife Helpline. Our crew handles the raccoon, snake, bat, and rodent work on the same streets.

Wilmington.wildlife_intro:
Wilmington's port-city mix drives its calls: raccoons and squirrels across the historic canopy neighborhoods, bats in the older housing, rats around the port and downtown corridors, and marsh-edge animals in the low neighborhoods.

Alligators occur in the river, Greenfield Lake, and the area's ponds — coexistence and the Wildlife Helpline cover them — while cottonmouths work the marsh and creek edges, and storm surge periodically floods the low streets' wildlife into their houses.

The coastal year in Wilmington runs mild and long. Raccoons den in spring, bats colonize attics through a summer protected by North Carolina's August 1 through April 30 eviction window for licensed Wildlife Control Agents, and ground-level animals — opossums, rodents, snakes — stay active through winters too warm to stop them. Storm season overlays everything, pushing marsh and river animals into the first dry structures. Our crew starts with a full inspection, then removes the animals and seals every entry we find, because closing only the obvious hole rarely holds.
